claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed, largely iron-based passive oxide film.
The native oxide film on Q235 contains trace Mn.
Q235 has a Mn-enriched surface sub-layer beneath or within its passive oxide.
Selective Mn dissolution modulates the stability of Q235's passive oxide during high-temperature molten-salt exposure.
A Mn-enriched sub-layer acts as a redox buffer that stabilizes the protective oxide.
Loss of Mn weakens the proposed redox-buffer layer and accelerates corrosion.
Preserving Mn at the oxide surface promotes corrosion resistance.
Mn can dissolve rapidly from an alloy into molten FLiBe at 700 °C.
At elevated temperatures, Mn in the Q235 passive film diffuses and dissolves into molten salt more rapidly than Fe.
Removing Mn from the surface destabilizes the oxide scale by disrupting the interfacial redox environment.
Samples with substantial Mn depletion will exhibit greater mass loss, deeper penetration, and poorer oxide integrity than Mn-retaining samples.
Q235 tested at room temperature or under inert conditions will undergo negligible Mn dissolution and retain a stable passive film with minimal corrosion.
The proposed Mn-dissolution mechanism is primarily operative in high-temperature molten-salt environments.
At lower temperature or under non-saline corrosion conditions, Mn dissolution is too slow to substantially alter the film.
Direct Fe oxidation may dominate Q235 degradation outside the high-temperature molten-salt regime.
Controlled oxidation can be used to prepare a Mn-rich Q235 surface intended to enhance Mn retention.
The proposed exposure uses FLiBe containing approximately 65% LiF and 35% BeF2 at 700–900 °C.
